sections.title: Introduction
sections.extract: Automated repository-level issue resolution has emerged as a criti- cal challenge in software engineering. The task aims to automat- ically localize and fix the defective code snippets, based on re- ported issues. In software development, developers spend a major- ity of their debugging efforts in understanding code and making changes [15, 52]. sections.title: Motivation
sections.extract: Repository-level issue resolution reveals the fundamental limited observation scope that agentic approaches face in complex software engineering scenarios [5, 7]. While individual agents can success- fully handle straightforward localization tasks, they systematically fail when multiple code locations appear relevant to issue descrip- tions, requiring comprehensive architectural understanding and careful evaluation

sections.title: Fault Propagation Traces Proposal
sections.extract: Since issue descriptions rarely pinpoint exact modification loca- tions, agents need to identify the fault propagation trace for issue resolution. To enable competitive fault localization, our algorithm generates multiple candidate fault propagation traces as localiza- tion proposals, followed by a competitive multi-agent debate to select the most promising trace. sections.extract: Multi-agent systems have emerged as a promising approach for complex problem-solving by leveraging diverse specialized per- spectives and collaborative reasoning. In software engineering contexts, these systems have shown success across various tasks including code generation [12, 41], automated testing and debug- ging [11, 34]. sections.title: Conclusion
sections.extract: In this paper, we presented SWE-Debate, a competitive multi-agent debate framework that addresses the agents’ limited observation scope problem in repository-level issue resolution. Our approach combines graph-based fault propagation trace generation with structured multi-agent debates to systematically evaluate compet- ing localization hypotheses, overcoming the perspective limitations of single-agent methods.
